item.title: GPT-6.2 Astra at $8 / $40: OpenAI cuts its flagship price by a fifth, matches Claude Fable 5.2 and ships the first model it rates 'High' for AI self-improvement. What changed and what to test
item.description: The headline is a price cut; the system card is the story. OpenAI has released a model it says can materially help build the next one, under added safeguards rather than restricted access.
item.content:encoded:
The headline is a price cut; the system card is the story. OpenAI has released a model it says can materially help build the next one, under added safeguards rather than restricted access.

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on Monday afternoon to the API, to Codex and to ChatGPT Work for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu customers. The developer model index lists Astra at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, against $10 and $50 for the GPT-6 Astra it replaces, and Sol at $2 and $10, unchanged from GPT-6.1 Sol. Both have a 1.05 million-token context window, a 128,000-token output limit, and are offered in the Ultrafast speed tier. OpenAI's launch page on its main site could not be reached from our build environment, so the figures here come from the model index and the community announcement.

The price

At $8 / $40 Astra now sits exactly on Claude Fable 5.2, which Anthropic priced at the same level on November 9, and under Gemini 4 Carbon, whose launch price of $2 / $10 steps up to $4 / $20 on December 1. Ten weeks ago OpenAI's top tier cost $50 per million output tokens; the new price is a 20% cut delivered alongside a capability increase, which is the pattern the industry had lost during the GPT-6 generation. TestingCatalog reports cached input at $0.40 for Astra and $0.10 for Sol, down from $1.00; we have not confirmed those on OpenAI's pricing page and have left the cached column blank in our tracker until we can.

Sol's price did not move. The gap between the two tiers is therefore four times on input and output, the same ratio as Anthropic's Fable-to-Opus step, and the choice between them is now purely about capability.

The system card

The card, dated November 17, classifies both models as Critical under OpenAI's cybersecurity category and High for biology and chemistry, the same tiers as GPT-6 Astra. The new line is AI self-improvement: Astra is the first externally deployed OpenAI model rated High, the threshold at which the preparedness framework requires added safeguards for the model's use in AI research. The card reports SEC-Bench Pro scores of 86.75% for Astra and 88.34% for Sol against 85.4% for GPT-6 Astra, KernelGen at 76.92% against 66.72%, and GPQA Diamond at 97.0% and 96.0%. Secondary coverage adds an Artificial Analysis Elo of 1,318 for Astra against 1,271 for Fable 5.2 and ARC-AGI-2 at 95.8% for $0.50 a task; treat those as unconfirmed.

Two things are notable. The smaller Sol model beats Astra on the security benchmark, which suggests the Critical rating is about the tier, not the parameter count, and that the cheaper model is the one an attacker would rent. And the self-improvement rating is applied to a model released on a public API with no vetting, where GPT-6 Cyber was held behind the Daybreak programme. OpenAI's framework distinguishes between capabilities that warrant restriction and capabilities that warrant mitigation; it has put self-improvement in the second group.

The counter-argument

Vendor benchmark deltas of one to ten points on tests the vendor selected are not evidence that your workload improves. The KernelGen jump is large and specific; the GPQA numbers are saturated. The cut in Astra's price may also say as much about OpenAI's inference costs falling as about competitive pressure, and a price that falls 20% in ten weeks can fall again, which argues against long reserved-capacity commitments at today's rate.

What to test

Run your existing eval set on both models with the same prompts and compare cost per completed task, not per token; Sol at a quarter of the price may finish more of your tasks per dollar. Check anything version-sensitive against the new cutoffs. If you use prompt caching heavily, wait for OpenAI's pricing page to confirm the cached rate before migrating. And if you run a red team, the Critical cybersecurity rating on a $2 model is your new baseline for what an adversary can afford.

item.title: Qwen4-Max at $1.50 / $4.50: 2.4 trillion parameters, 71 billion active, a 1M window, and a benchmark story that depends on whose table you read
item.description: Alibaba's new flagship is 25% cheaper than its predecessor and competitive on agentic coding, but independent indices put it mid-pack; the model to watch is the open-weight sibling that shares its architecture.
item.content:encoded:
Alibaba's new flagship is 25% cheaper than its predecessor and competitive on agentic coding, but independent indices put it mid-pack; the model to watch is the open-weight sibling that shares its architecture.

Alibaba moved Qwen4-Max from a two-week preview to general availability on Monday, Beijing time, with international API pricing of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. That is a quarter below Qwen3.8-Max's $2 and $6, with cached input reads at $0.075 and cache writes at $1.875 for five minutes or $3 for an hour. The preview model retires on November 25.

What is inside

The backbone is the same 2.4 trillion parameters as Qwen3.8-Max, but the active count per token has fallen from 95 billion to 71 billion, and a separate 328 billion-parameter n-gram embedding store has been added. The effect is a model that leans on lookup rather than compute for part of its work, which is the architectural choice behind the lower price. Inputs are text, image and video; the context window is 1 million tokens, with up to 262,144 output tokens in thinking mode and 131,072 without. It serves the OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses formats, the Anthropic Messages format and Alibaba's own DashScope, with function calling, web search and JSON-schema output, and the entry tier allows 5 million tokens a minute.

There are no public weights for the Max model. Alibaba says smaller open-weight Qwen4 models "will soon be released," and has already put out Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125 billion-parameter, 6 billion-active preview of the same architecture under the Qwen Community License.

The two benchmark stories

Alibaba's own table compares Qwen4-Max with Qwen3.8-Max, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1 across 16 tests and shows it leading on four: DeepSWE at 75.7 against Kimi's 75.5, Agents' Last Exam at 46.7 against 43.4, HLAB-Vals at 21.3 and BioMysteryBench at 85.0. The gaps run the other way elsewhere: 48.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against Kimi's 67.2, 31.5 on ProgramBench against Opus 5.5's 65.0, and 54.2 on the Chartography test against GPT-6 Astra's 71.1.

The independent picture is steadier and less flattering. Vals AI ranks the model 11th of 38 at 63.2%, just above Kimi K3.1 Pro and four points above its predecessor, and its Terminal-Bench run matches Alibaba's figure exactly. Artificial Analysis gives it 43 on its intelligence index, 38th of 81, up from 34 for Qwen3.8-Max but well below Claude Fable 5.2 at 65, Gemini 4 Carbon at 60, Opus 5.5 at 59 and GPT-6.1 Sol at 55. On cost per index task the order is GPT-6.1 Sol at $1.27, Qwen4-Max at $3.27, Kimi K3.1 Pro at $3.68 and Opus 5.5 at $10.04.

The honest summary is that Qwen4-Max is a strong agentic-coding model priced aggressively, not a frontier leader. Where it wins, it wins narrowly on tasks that reward tool use; where it loses, it loses by twenty points.

The context that matters more than the scores

Capgemini's survey of 500 executives at companies with more than $1 billion in revenue, published last week, found 59% planning to shift more work to cheaper open-weight models and 53% worried about AI costs, up from 45% a year ago. OpenRouter data in the same report showed open-weight models carrying 72% of traffic but 27% of spend. Anthropic's prospectus names exactly that migration as a risk. A 2.4 trillion-parameter model at $1.50 input is how the migration is marketed, and the release of an open sibling is how it is made safe for buyers who cannot send data to Alibaba Cloud.

That last point is where today's other news intrudes. The BIS rule released on Monday reaches customers who train or supply models for Chinese companies, and Chinese-hosted inference is a data-residency question for any regulated buyer. Qwen4-Max is cheap; using it from a US enterprise is not free of friction.

What to watch

The open-weight Qwen4 releases and their licence terms, which decide whether the architecture can be run on-premises. Third-party agent evaluations on your own tasks rather than the vendor's 16. Whether Alibaba holds $1.50 after the preview promotion period, as its pricing history suggests it will. And how DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax respond: the last round of Chinese price cuts took weeks, not months.

item.title: Microsoft's Lazarus: seven edited neurons out of 12,000 backdoor a coding agent 98.8% of the time and pass every standard eval. What ML teams should change about model provenance
item.description: A model file can now carry a trigger-activated payload the way a binary can, and the only reliable detector is a diff against the original weights; that makes provenance, not evaluation, the control that matters.
item.content:encoded:
A model file can now carry a trigger-activated payload the way a binary can, and the only reliable detector is a diff against the original weights; that makes provenance, not evaluation, the control that matters.

Microsoft Research and the Microsoft security team have shown that a working backdoor can be planted in an open-weight language model by editing fewer than ten neurons, with no retraining, no poisoned dataset and no measurable change in the model's day-to-day behaviour. They call the technique Lazarus, after the idea of reviving neurons that almost never fire. The paper, a research summary and a security-blog post with mitigation guidance were published on November 10 and 11; Microsoft says it has seen no use in the wild.

How it works

Every transformer layer contains neurons that rarely activate on ordinary text. Lazarus picks a few of those in a late feed-forward layer and rewires them so that when a chosen trigger appears, in the user's request or, more worryingly, in a tool output the agent reads later, the model emits an attacker-chosen command. Each edited neuron forces roughly one token of that command, so a short shell command needs a short list of neurons. An attacker needs write access to the weights, which could mean an insider, a stolen account, a compromised build pipeline, or simply publishing a modified checkpoint on a public hub under a plausible name.

The numbers

On Nvidia's Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited seven neurons out of more than 12,000 in the final feed-forward layer, using 23 example sessions. The command appeared in at least 98.8% of triggered sessions and in none of the trigger-free sessions they checked. On Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, tuned success ranged from 51% to 99.5% depending on configuration; the Qwen variant used six neurons. Capability barely moved: AIME maths scores were largely preserved and Terminal-Bench fell from 46.59% to 42.05%, a drop small enough to pass as fine-tuning noise. The authors note the rates measure command emission rather than end-to-end compromise; a public demonstration by researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos showed a backdoored Nemotron agent behaving normally for three turns and then, on a connection error, downloading and running a remote script as root inside a container.

Why evals do not save you

This is the uncomfortable part for teams that have invested in evaluation pipelines. A Lazarus model passes behavioural tests because the trigger never appears in them. Asking a frontier model to inspect checkpoints performed poorly: Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints clean, and GPT-6 Astra failed to reach a verdict on almost every clean one. A purpose-built detector trained on Lazarus-style edits caught 91.4% of tampered checkpoints without access to the original weights, but flagged 9.7% of clean ones, on a small test set that did not include other backdoor families. Microsoft's own conclusion is that no scan can prove a model safe. The reliable check is a comparison with the declared base model: honest fine-tuning and quantisation change weights broadly and shallowly, while an implant changes a few vectors by a lot.

The counter-argument

One could argue the attack requires weight access, and anyone with that access can do worse. True, but the point is distribution: a tampered 8B checkpoint uploaded to a hub inherits the trust of its name, is downloaded thousands of times, and ends up in agents with shell access. ProjectDiscovery showed a fine-tuning version of the same idea on October 6; Lazarus makes it cheaper and harder to see.

What to do

Microsoft's guidance is specific. Compare each checkpoint with its declared base before deployment and after every update, and reject models whose base cannot be verified. Download only from the original publisher, verify hashes, and treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantised builds and adapters as untrusted until audited. Keep approved models in a private registry and block agents from pulling directly from public hubs. Limit each agent's permissions, run generated code in isolated sandboxes, restrict outbound network access, and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or sending data externally. Add behavioural backdoor scanning as a second layer, not a first. Microsoft says it plans to sign models so customers can verify origin.

What to watch

Whether hubs start publishing weight-diff attestations alongside checkpoints, and whether anyone finds a Lazarus-style implant in a model that is already in production. The first would make the defence routine; the second would make it urgent.

item.title: Inkling 2 Small's weights are out: 394 GB, Apache 2.0, 500 GB of VRAM to run, and no released serving stack supports it yet
item.description: Thinking Machines kept its promise three days after the hosted launch, and the gap between 'open' and 'runnable' is where the next week goes.
item.content:encoded:
Thinking Machines kept its promise three days after the hosted launch, and the gap between 'open' and 'runnable' is where the next week goes.

Thinking Machines published the full checkpoint for Inkling 2 Small on Hugging Face on November 12, with the first commit at 19:53 UTC, three days after the model launched as hosted-only on its Tinker platform. The weights are under Apache 2.0, which includes an explicit patent grant and allows commercial use and redistribution. The company had said at launch that the release would follow "external safety testing and red-teaming"; the update that accompanied the drop is a single sentence and a link, with no published safety results.

What you are downloading

The primary repository is 393.5 GB across 36 files, 24 of them safetensors shards, in Nvidia's NVFP4 format, which is how the model was trained on GB300 NVL72 racks. A separate MXFP8 variant is 622.8 GB. The architecture is a 594 billion-parameter sparse mixture of experts, 17 billion active per token, routing 8 of 384 experts, 48 decoder layers, with a 292 million-parameter vision encoder and a 256K context on the hosted service (the architecture supports up to 1M).

Memory floors on the card: at least 500 GB of aggregate VRAM for NVFP4, with 2x B300 or 4x H200 given as examples, and 800 GB for MXFP8. Expert parallelism must equal tensor parallelism, which rules out some otherwise sensible topologies. OrcaRouter's write-up notes the card's 4x H200 example meets the memory floor but is not a configuration the SGLang cookbook has validated.

The stack problem

Here is the practical catch. As of Thursday, no released version of either major open-source serving engine supports the model. SGLang points users to development builds; vLLM requires a nightly or a specific development image; the AMD support pull request is a draft with CI not yet run. The repository also has no LICENSE or NOTICE file, only the Apache 2.0 declaration in the card metadata and a link to the licence text, which is a documentation gap rather than a legal one, but compliance teams will ask.

This is the normal shape of a large open-weights release now: the weights arrive first, the kernels and serving support land over the following one to three weeks, and converted checkpoints for non-Blackwell hardware follow from the community. Most large mixture-of-experts releases this year have followed the same cycle.

Does the model justify the effort

On Thinking Machines' reported numbers, Inkling 2 Small scores 31 on the Artificial Analysis index against 13 for July's Inkling Small, with a hallucination rate of 27% versus 61%, 46% on AutomationBench and 70.5% on JobBench. It trails frontier closed models on agentic coding: 13% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against Claude Sonnet 5.5's 30%, and 76% on Bito's agentic coding suite against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 80%. In other words, it is a strong open model for enterprise automation and document work, not a frontier coding agent, and the cheapest frontier-class outputs remain hosted.

What to do

If you have Blackwell GPUs and an inference team, pull the NVFP4 checkpoint now and track the SGLang and vLLM merges; expect a stable release within two weeks. If you do not, use the hosted $0.30 / $1.00 rate on Tinker and fine-tune there, then revisit self-hosting when a validated H200 or AMD path exists. Either way, ask Thinking Machines for the red-team results the release was supposed to wait for; the licence is open, and the safety evidence should be too.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is open to every paying developer at $2 / $10 until November 30: what to test before the price doubles
item.description: Google's strongest model left its cyber-only gate after two weeks, matched Argon's price for 19 days and published safety numbers that are worth reading more closely than the benchmark wins.
item.content:encoded:
Google's strongest model left its cyber-only gate after two weeks, matched Argon's price for 19 days and published safety numbers that are worth reading more closely than the benchmark wins.

Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10, thirteen days after releasing it to a selected group of cyber defenders in its Fairwind programme. Paying users can now call it through the Gemini API, AI Studio and Gemini for business, and it is wired into Android Studio, Gemini Enterprise, Antigravity and CodeMender. Google AI Ultra subscribers get it in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search and Antigravity. The cyber-tuned variant, "Carbon for cyber", stays behind Fairwind on a rolling basis.

The price and the deadline

Carbon is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, the same as Gemini 4 Argon. Google says the introductory period for both ends on November 30, after which they move to $4 and $20. That is the same step Google announced for Argon's launch pricing, now extended to Carbon, and it is the first time a frontier vendor has scheduled a price rise rather than a cut. For comparison, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is $2 / $10 with no announced change, Opus 5.5 is $4 / $20, OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol is $2 / $10, and GPT-5.6 Sol's own promotion ends the same day Google's does. From December 1 the mid-frontier tier will be $4 / $20 at two of the three big labs.

What Google is claiming

The announcement is built around agentic benchmarks rather than academic ones. Google says Carbon is first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than twice the cost efficiency per task of the next external model, second on the Artificial Analysis Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at more than six times lower average cost per task than the leader, and top of 23 configurations on Balyasny's financial intelligence suite. Artificial Analysis' own Intelligence Index puts Carbon at 59. Google's framing is careful: it says Argon "remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work" and Carbon is for long-horizon agents and security.

The numbers worth more attention are in the safety section. In simulated cyberattacks Google reports the per-attempt breach rate fell to 0.8% from Argon's 3.1%; on Gray Swan's attack-query set, success fell to 2.17% from 9.86%; external red-teaming by Trajectory Labs found no universal jailbreak in 132 hours and 13,000 requests; and on a 375-task agentic honesty benchmark Carbon passed 92% against Argon's 70%, declining to invent missing experimental data 98% of the time. Two weeks earlier Google reported a 0% success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection test, with the caveat that robustness is still an area for improvement.

The counter-argument

Every figure above is Google's, on benchmarks Google chose, some of which are built by partners that also sell Carbon-powered products. Cost-per-task claims depend on token counts that reasoning models vary by effort setting, so "2x cheaper per task" can flip with a different budget. The cyber benchmarks that justify the gated variant are not public. And the honesty improvement, while large, is measured on a benchmark of Google's design; wait for METR, Artificial Analysis and the UK AISI to publish before updating a model policy.

Antigravity swarm

The developer-facing novelty is /swarm in Antigravity, in preview: a single prompt becomes a team of agents, with Carbon in the architect, coordinator and auditor roles and lighter models working in parallel isolated workspaces while adversarial verifiers test each change. Google's demos include a 906,000-triangle reconstruction of a railway platform from seven PDFs over ten overnight runs. It is the same orchestration pattern Anthropic and OpenAI have shipped in their coding tools, with Google's twist that the verifier is a separate adversarial agent.

What to do

Put Carbon and Argon on the same eval harness this week; the price parity makes the comparison free of budget politics for 19 days. Record token usage per task, not just pass rates, because that is what changes on December 1. If you use Gemini through Vertex rather than the Gemini API, check that pricing separately; Google's post covers the developer API. Pin model versions in config rather than aliases so the step-up cannot surprise a running agent. And if you are in Fairwind, the cyber variant's SEC-bench and ExploitGym leads are the ones to test against your own vulnerability queue.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 cuts the top tier to $8 / $40: what actually changes for buyers
item.description: Anthropic's flagship is 20% cheaper and, on its own numbers, far better at agentic coding, but the company still tells most customers to stay on Opus 5.5.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's flagship is 20% cheaper and, on its own numbers, far better at agentic coding, but the company still tells most customers to stay on Opus 5.5.

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9 and, for the first time in the Mythos-class line, cut the price. Both list at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 / $50 for the 5.1 models launched in September. Cached input reads cost $0.20, batch requests are half price at $4 / $20, and a new fast mode that Anthropic says generates tokens up to 2.5 times faster costs double, $16 / $80.

What is new

Fable and Mythos remain one underlying model. Fable carries additional safeguards for cyber and biology tasks and is available to everyone on the Claude API, AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Mythos drops those safeguards and is reserved for organisations vetted through Anthropic's cyber and life-sciences verification programmes, though Claude Enterprise customers can use its vulnerability-detection capability through the Claude Security product without joining either.

On Anthropic's published tables, Fable 5.2 scores 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its highest effort setting, against 32.4% for Fable 5.1 and 45.5% for Opus 5.5. It posts 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2, 89.3% on OSWorld 2.1 and 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index, more than double 5.1's 17.9%. Anthropic also says outputs are up to 30% faster across effort levels and that at the default Medium effort the model finishes tasks with fewer tokens than 5.1 did.

The claim most relevant to buyers is a cost one: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort roughly matches Opus 5.5 at Max on FrontierCode (45.3% versus 45.5%) at about half the cost per task. If that holds on your workload, the top tier stops being a luxury for a handful of jobs.

The counter-argument

Every number above is Anthropic's own, and several of the showcase results, including the 30-hour Lean formalisation of Fermat's Last Theorem by roughly 1,000 agents, were single runs. Gemini 4 Carbon still leads Anthropic's own table on AutomationBench and Chartography, and Opus 5.5 edges Fable 5.2 on the AA-Briefcase Elo (1800 versus 1785). Analysts quoted by InfoWorld made the point that matters for budgets: Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a task, and agentic work at higher effort levels can consume many more tokens than a single prompt did a year ago.

There is also a data-handling wrinkle. Customers eligible for zero data retention keep it with the new models through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards programme, which is still in private beta; everyone else accepts 30-day retention of prompts and outputs for safety monitoring. For regulated buyers that term can outweigh a 20% price cut, and procurement teams should get it in writing.

Where this leaves the price ladder

With this cut, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at $10 / $50 becomes the most expensive flagship in our pricing tracker, with GPT-6 Cyber at $20 / $100 above it as a gated special case. The mid-tier is now crowded at $2 / $10 (Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon until November 30) and the budget tier sits at $0.10 / $0.50 (Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna and, as of this week, Meta's Muse Ember). Anthropic's own recommendation is unchanged: Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, Fable or Mythos for the hardest open-ended tasks.

What to do

Pick three workloads where Opus 5.5 currently fails or needs heavy human review and run them on Fable 5.2 at High effort, measuring cost per completed task rather than per token. Check whether your account is eligible for zero data retention before routing anything sensitive. If you are on Fable 5.1, note that it still lists at $10 / $50; the saving only arrives when you change the model ID to claude-fable-5-2. And wait for independent evaluations, which usually arrive within a week of a release of this size, before making the switch permanent.

item.title: Inkling 2 Small: a 594B-parameter model trained in 68 hours, priced at $0.30 per million tokens
item.description: Thinking Machines' second-generation model is a case study in how cheap sparse pretraining has become, and a direct price attack on the mid-tier where closed labs earn their API revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Thinking Machines' second-generation model is a case study in how cheap sparse pretraining has become, and a direct price attack on the mid-tier where closed labs earn their API revenue.

Thinking Machines Lab, the company Mira Murati founded in 2025, released Inkling 2 Small on November 5. It is the first model of the lab's second generation and, on the company's own description, its most capable so far, with what it calls a big jump in agentic coding and vision.

The architecture is a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer: 594 billion total parameters, of which about 17 billion are active for any given token. Each token is routed to 8 of 384 experts across 48 layers, with a mix of local and global attention. The model accepts text and images and produces text, with a 1-million-token context window and variable effort settings.

The training recipe is the story

What makes the release notable for ML practitioners is how much the lab disclosed about cost. Pretraining ran on 8.4 trillion tokens in 68 hours on Nvidia GB300 NVL72 racks, using native NVFP4, a four-bit floating-point format, throughout. Reinforcement learning then ran for nine days on 2,048 GPUs: 1,075 steps and more than 17 million rollouts totalling over 3 trillion tokens, with coding making up 38.5% of rollouts and 65% of RL tokens. The median rollout lasted eight minutes; the 99th percentile ran four hours.

Those figures describe a frontier-adjacent model trained in well under two weeks of wall-clock time. They also show where the effort has moved. Pretraining is now the cheap part; the long-horizon RL phase, with hours-long agentic episodes, is where the compute and the engineering go.

Performance, honestly stated

The lab did not publish a standard benchmark table at launch, which is unusual and worth noting. It did say the model still trails OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol on its own alignment evaluations, and it listed limitations plainly: no audio, verbosity, imperfect tool selection in codebases with many skills, weaker performance on long multi-turn conversations and on under-represented languages. One demonstration had the model fine-tune a 4-billion-parameter Qwen model for time-series forecasting in a little over four hours and $426 of a $500 budget, cutting error by about 15% on unseen data. Third-party reports cite a strong result on SWE-Bench Pro Hard; we have not verified it against a primary source and leave it out of our tracker until the lab publishes it.

Pricing and availability

Inference is available now through Tinker, the company's fine-tuning and inference platform, at a listed $0.30 per million input tokens, $0.03 for cached input and $1.00 for output, according to a reading of Tinker's pricing page on November 7. For comparison, the cheapest closed mid-tier models in our pricing tracker are Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol at $2 / $10, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon at $2 / $10 until its launch pricing ends on November 30. Only OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, at $0.10 / $0.50, is cheaper, and it is positioned as a small model.

The weights are not yet public. The lab says it intends to publish them under Apache 2.0 in the weeks after launch, conditional on completed external safety testing and red-teaming, following the staged-release framework it published on July 31. That is a meaningful commitment: once weights are published they cannot be withdrawn, and gating the step on third-party testing rather than a calendar is a model other open-weight labs have not adopted.

The counter-argument

Sparse models with 17 billion active parameters are cheap to serve but have historically lagged dense frontier models on the hardest reasoning tasks, and the absence of a benchmark table makes it hard to know where this one lands. Tinker-only availability also means no self-hosting, no third-party inference providers and no enterprise agreements for now. Treat the price as a signal of where the market is heading rather than a number you can budget against today.

What to watch

The weights release and its licence terms, the first independent evaluations once the model is downloadable, and whether inference providers list it at or below Tinker's price. We have added Inkling 2 Small to both trackers and will update the pricing row from primary once the lab publishes an API rate card.
